description: Maps every area of the repository to the code it owns and the documentation that governs it, so 'which docs govern this change?' always has a machine-readable answer. This file is committed data guarded by an admission test: scripts/check-area-map.js fails CI when the map goes stale (a pattern matching no tracked file, an entry pointing at an untracked file), when a tracked file resolves to no area and is neither a repo-wide doc nor a justified exception, or when any tracked .md doc (anywhere in the repo, not only under docs/) is placed in no area's doc set, repo-wide list, or justified 'unassigned' exception — being matched only by a code pattern is not a doc home. An 'unassigned' exception earns its keep file by file: an entry no covered file needs is unnecessary as a whole, and a covered file that resolves anyway while other covered files still need the entry is reported on its own, so the entry is narrowed to the files that need it. An area owns code, a doc set, or both: a docs-only area (no code) is valid when it carries a non-empty doc set. An area earns its place by supplying something the rest of the map does not — docs some tracked file's governing set would otherwise lose, or coverage some tracked file would otherwise lack: an area whose deletion — with every 'area:<name>' reference to it first inlined to the docs it stands for, so what is asked is what the area supplies rather than whether a declaration names it — leaves every tracked file governed by exactly the same docs, and none of them unowned, makes no contribution the rest of the map does not already make. Each area is judged on its own against the rest of the map, never as a set: areas that supply the same docs each answer for the others, so each is named and each removal is a new question the next run answers. Patterns support '*', '**', and {a,b} alternation only, in every list of this map that states one: an area's 'code' patterns, the 'unassigned' exceptions, the 'declared-governance' declarations, and the 'governance-partitions' trees. In each of them a pattern must describe the tree through every alternative it expands to — braces expand to the cross product of their groups, so what is held is what a pattern expands to rather than what its entry visibly spells: every expansion must match at least one tracked file, an expansion matching nothing beside siblings that still match is stale on its own and the entry is rewritten until each expansion matches, and an entry with no live expansion left is stale as a whole. Doc entries are literal tracked paths, never patterns. Code files and docs are many-to-many: a file or doc may belong to several areas. A code file may also name a governing doc directly with a '// see docs/<path>.md' comment, which adds every area whose doc set contains that doc. A file may instead DECLARE its complete governing doc set with a 'declared-governance' entry (a required 'governed-by' array — [] states the governing set is empty): that declared set governs the file's disposition in place of the docs its covering code area would supply, and area membership and '// see' pointers add nothing more. A declared file keeps the code-area coverage its patterns give it (a declaration grants no coverage of its own), and its governance is declared once and from one source (a declared file is not also a repo-wide doc, nor does it carry a '// see' pointer into a doc set). Each element of a 'governed-by' array is either a literal tracked doc path or an 'area:<name>' reference standing for that area's whole doc set, which it expands to — the compositional way to say a file owes an area's doctrine as a unit, with any further doc named as a literal beside it. 'governance-partitions' lists the trees whose files each declare their own governance, one entry per tree stating the 'pattern' that names the tree and the 'reason' its files declare one by one: every tracked file matching one of those patterns carries a declared-governance entry, so a file added there states its subject rather than inheriting the union its tree ride supplies, and a partition pattern matching no tracked file is stale. Inside a partitioned tree, a declaration stating exactly what the covering areas supply is the honest answer and is kept as such; outside one, that same statement adds nothing and is redundant — read file by file, so an entry stating nothing new for every file it answers for is redundant as a whole, while one stating nothing new for some of those files is reported on them and splits. Each side therefore reads the same declaration differently, so a declared-governance entry belongs to one side of a boundary: an entry matching both partition-covered files and files outside every partition is refused, and splits at the boundary.

repo-wide.description: Docs that apply to every area of the repository — a change anywhere can be governed by them. They resolve in their own right and do not need to belong to an area's doc set (though some also do).

unassigned.reason: License text — not project documentation and owned by no area.
Contributor license agreement — project governance, not area documentation.
Shipped end-user assets (icons, the reading guide delivered with dispatch payloads) — product artifacts, not project documentation.

Security policy — coordinated-disclosure governance (how a vulnerability is reported and fixed), referenced from .github/CONTRIBUTING.md; a process/governance doc, not code-governing area documentation.
Code of Conduct (Contributor Covenant) — community governance, not area documentation.
Pull-request body template — contribution scaffolding whose rules live in .github/CONTRIBUTING.md; a form, not area documentation.
Reference-implementations index — orientation for runnable example artifacts (never shipped in a release), not project doctrine.
Reference sync-server README — implementation notes for a runnable example artifact (never shipped); the protocol it implements is governed by docs/api/sync-protocol.md.

governance-partitions.reason: The shared test tree sits under tree-wide code patterns from both the format area and the sync area, so a file added there is born owing both doc sets at once — the shared-core architecture, the session format, both wire protocols, and the user guides — and a file under the fixture subtree owes the fixture area's docs on top of them. Each file states the subject it actually exercises instead.

The Tauri crate's test directory sits under tree-wide code patterns from both the desktop capture area and the desktop test area, so a file added there is born owing both doc sets at once. Each file states the contract it pins instead, named per entry.

declared-governance.reason: Registered-clause verification data — records keyed to clause ids, consumed by the docs-disposition check and validated by scripts/check-clause-registry.js.
Unit tests for the CI-machinery check scripts — they exercise the check tooling itself; their contract is the behaviour of the scripts under test, and the unit-suite orientation lists them.
cargo-mutants configuration — the desktop crate's Rust mutation-run settings; the CI guide states its scoping role, so an edit here primes that claim too.

cargo-deny configuration — the desktop crate's license/advisory policy; the CI guide states its configuring role in the audit gate, so an edit here primes that claim rather than the shell doctrine its directory would supply.
Codecov configuration — coverage-report and status settings; the CI guide states which of its statuses gate and which are informational, so an edit here primes those claims too.

The root manifest — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, its scripts map is the subject of demands both verification documents make of it: the corpus doctrine states which flags each platform's corpus gate command carries and when (and the verification-inventory lint holds that command against the doctrine), and the sufficiency-lint doc names the sufficiency:check script as the executing home of the standing corpus's root list. So a scripts-map edit primes those two documents beside the CI set. Dependency-only diffs are recognised by the disposition check on their own and stay exempt, so the amplification lands on real script and engine edits.
Stryker configuration — JavaScript mutation-testing settings; the CI guide states their thresholds.break role, so an edit here primes that claim too.
The shared-code copy mechanism — its copy model, outputs, and freshness rule are owned by the shared-core architecture doc.
The shared-views injection — the one-fragment-two-shells assembly the shared-core architecture doc owns.

Format-subject unit suites — they exercise the shared format modules and schema tooling, and the regression suite pins the session model's own history behaviour; their contract is the format area's doctrine as a unit, not the sync protocol their tree-mates ride, and the unit-suite orientation lists them.
The backward-compatibility harness — the compat doc owns its discovery and baseline rules, the format doc's stamp-relaxation clause cites it, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.
The sufficiency baseline lock — the lint doc owns the both-direction locking and regeneration rules it enforces, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.
The conformance-vector locks — they guard clauses of the locator procedure, the corpus doctrine, and the format doc's measurement clause, and the unit-suite orientation lists them.
The no-shipped-resolver guard — it enforces the locator doc's never-an-implementation rule and the corpus doctrine's inert-vector posture, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.
The vector measurement modules — they implement the locator doc's per-strategy query semantics for the harnesses.
The comparator's unit suite — the corpus doctrine owns the comparison classes and refusal rules it pins, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

Unit tests for CI machinery (the docs-disposition audit, the next-release-version tool, the lint-script glob-quoting guard) plus the schema-artifact size budget — the unit-suite orientation lists each of them and states what it covers, while the budget's thresholds and the tooling contracts stay the suites' own, so that orientation is the whole governing set.

UI-subject unit suites — they exercise the shared panel fragment's rendering, the conflict-view module, and simple-mode step creation and rendering; their contract is the panel-ui area's doctrine as a unit, not the sync/format union their tree ride supplies. They also build and render the format's step records (logical_id, step_number, step_type/expect) and pin the canonical active-view resolution the render module reuses, so the session-format doc governs them beside the panel-ui set, and the unit-suite orientation lists them.

Sync chokepoints implementing the format's step-history and field-shape rules — its committed format pointer would, after the schema-contract split, drag that area's locator and taxonomy docs onto a module that emits no locators; this declaration states its true governors: its areas' docs plus the format doc the pointer names.

The conflict-view module — both a sync-state consumer and the panel fragment's resolution view — its committed format pointer would, after the schema-contract split, drag that area's locator and taxonomy docs onto a module that emits no locators; this declaration states its true governors: its areas' docs plus the format doc the pointer names.

The shared rendering module — resolves and renders the committed step history for the panel fragment — its committed format pointer would, after the schema-contract split, drag that area's locator and taxonomy docs onto a module that emits no locators; this declaration states its true governors: its areas' docs plus the format doc the pointer names.

The stamp-gate suite — its subject is the format area's doctrine, whose whole doc set it owes as a unit, and it pins the sync protocol's skip-and-report mismatch handling over the format's version stamp, so the sync-protocol doc its citing clause (SP-8) names governs it too, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The composition suite — its subject is the format area's doctrine, whose whole doc set it owes as a unit; beyond it, it is the registry-cited guard for the locator (LR-24), extension-capture (ECP-10), and sufficiency (SL-4) clauses over the composed schemas, so each of those docs is named here beside the format set, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The extension panel — its committed format pointer would drag the schema-contract set onto a module that emits no locators; this declaration states its true governors: the sidepanel area's docs plus the format doc its commit logic implements.

The CI hub workflow — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set it implements the shared-core freshness gate, the Rust test self-classification, the coverage staging topology, the release process's platform-scoped call and secret contracts, the corpus doctrine's producer/differ job topology and pinned-image rule, the job and posture claims the sufficiency-lint doc's entry-points table states, and the job ids that BOTH verification documents' job cites are pinned against by the verification-inventory admission test.
The weekly mutation workflow — the mutation-strategy doc owns its cadence and threshold posture.

The desktop command-surface admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, the application-shell doc's command-table clause is verified by it, per its registry row, and its mock-surface leg implements the integration-suite doc's serviced-command contract. Its exported comment-stripped and string-blanked Rust views also serve the clause-registry check, which resolves a row's named test cases against the declarations a cited Rust file states, so an edit to them changes what that gate holds a registry row's test-case field to.

The test-inventory lint and the shared doc-scan primitives (fence model, clause-section slice, table parse, list/token readers) the surface checks verify their clauses through — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, an edit here changes what the gate holds the registered suite inventories, coverage lists, and mutation kill sets to (the suite docs, the coverage doc, and the mutation doc, whose mutate-scope table this gate holds to the cargo-mutants config), and what the surface checks' clauses are checked against (the clause docs; the desktop suite doc is doubly coupled — its mock serviced-command leg runs on this file's list reader, a coupling DSH-1's registry row records as held by the check itself). Those same token primitives also serve the clause-registry check, which resolves a row's named test cases against the declarators a cited JavaScript file states, so an edit to them changes what that gate holds a registry row's test-case field to. The same scanning rules render the offset-preserving blanked view the extension unit suite's absence guards read their sources through, so what this file leaves visible in that view is what those guards can still find. A clause citation into this file naming a doc this declaration already carries — the runtime and application-shell docs among them — rides the declaration; the rest are recorded, reasoned exceptions at the clause-governance check.

The verification-inventory admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, it holds the corpus doctrine's relaxation, normalization, and session-catalogue clauses and the sufficiency-lint doc's predicate tables to the constants and manifest they describe, per those clauses' registry rows, and holds both verification docs' job cites against .github/workflows/test.yml's job ids, so both verification docs govern it beside that set.

The extension-surface admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, the permissions doc's manifest clause and the runtime doc's dispatcher clause are verified by it, per their registry rows.

The capture-surface admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, both platform capture docs' surface-enumeration clauses name it as the check that holds them, and the core capture doc's inclusion-filter clause names it as added coverage, per their registry rows, so all three capture documents govern it beside that set.

The platform-adapter seam's admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, the shared-core doc's adapter-seam clause is verified by it, per that clause's registry row, so the shared-core architecture doc governs it beside that set; the adapter files it reads are its subject, not its doctrine.

The schema-echo admission test — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, the session-format doc's authority-ordering clause and its unknown-key posture clause (SF-1, SF-14) are verified by it, per their registry rows, so the format doc governs it beside that set; the surfaces it reads are its subject, not its doctrine.

The clause-citation governance lint — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit, and it is the home of the shared citation shape the schema-echo check reads the SF-1 register/row closure through, so an edit here changes what that clause is checked against and the format doc governs it beside that set.

The clause-registry parity check — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit, and it is the home of the shared split-and-edge shape every reader of a row's citations applies, the schema-echo check included, so an edit here changes how the SF-1 register/row closure is read and the format doc governs it beside that set.

The release-output guard — it owes the ci/release area's whole doc set as a unit; beyond that set, the feature-branch dist gate that the format doc's version-bump clause is verified by, per its registry row and the release process doc.

Committed release-output copies — regenerated by the release pipeline, hard-blocked in feature PRs by the release-output guard, and carried by the automation PR whose generated body has no disposition sections.
The lint configuration — beyond the CI guides and the contributing conventions it carries the registered guard of the extension capture doctrine's static-import clause (the no-dynamic-import rule).

Committed panel build outputs — each is assembled from a platform shell plus the single shared views fragment by the shared-code sync and is never hand-edited (edit the shell or the shared views source and re-run the sync). Their only invariant is that they match the regenerated assembly, which the shared-core doc owns (the one-fragment-two-shells assembly and the outputs-freshness rule); the platform behaviour docs their code areas would otherwise supply govern the platforms' code, not this generated HTML. Coverage is unchanged — each still resolves to its package area for the code-ownership totality check.

Sync-subject example and contract suites — they drive the sync client and its transport, scheduler, store, baseline, and resolution fixtures against a stubbed server; their contract is the sync area's doctrine as a unit — the protocol and dispatch specifications and the user-facing sync guides — and the unit-suite orientation lists them.

Sync-subject property suites — they drive detection, classification, resolution, scheduling, and the push/pull cycle over randomized histories and pin the protocol invariants the registry cites them for; their contract is the sync area's doctrine as a unit, and the unit-suite orientation lists them.

The sync-client suite — its subject is the sync area's doctrine as a unit, and the format doc is named beside it because the registry's known-field pull-projection row (SF-13) cites this suite's regression cases as its guard, so a change here bears on that clause; the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The attention-indicator derivation suite — it pins which Units the panels badge for attention, how each is labelled Review or Conflict, and which row it belongs on; that badge contract is the panel-ui area's doctrine, which it owes as a unit, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The payload contract suite — it validates dispatch payloads and export data against the composed platform schemas, so its subject is the format area's doctrine as a unit, and the dispatch doc its citing clause (DI-3) names governs the payload wrapper it builds; the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The shared security suite — each doc here is one of its subjects: escaping and the assembled panel pages' policy meta tags (the shared-core doc owns the fragment and the assembly), payload and export secrecy (the dispatch doc, whose DI-6 and DI-10 rows cite this suite), the export structure the format doc defines, the storage-key naming the persistence doc states, and the extension manifest's permissions and web-accessible resources the permissions doc enumerates. The unit-suite orientation lists it.

The shared data layer's time budgets — the suite pins how long active-view resolution, payload assembly, rendering, and reordering may take on large sessions. The unit-suite orientation lists it and states what it guards, while the thresholds themselves stay the suite's own, so that orientation is the whole governing set, on the same footing as the schema-artifact size budget.

The frozen per-platform recordings — the backward-compatibility harness validates them by shape and the sufficiency baseline is locked over them, so they owe the fixture area's whole doc set as a unit.

The sufficiency baseline — the recorded result of the static predicates over the frozen fixtures and the corpus truth files. It owes the fixture area's whole doc set as a unit: the sufficiency-lint doc owns its both-direction locking and its regeneration rule, and the backward-compat doc names it among this directory's residents, states how its plain .json suffix keeps it out of both discovery sweeps, and carries the command that regenerates it.

The minimal schema stub — it carries the pinned docent_format consts the payload and export builders read, so the format doc that defines that stamp governs it; and the backward-compat doc enumerates it among this directory's residents as unrelated to the corpus, stating what it is for and how its .js suffix keeps it out of both discovery sweeps. Those consts feed stamp derivation in the shared unit suites only — the sufficiency lint composes real platform schemas per its own input contract and never reads this file — so the lint's doc is not among its governors.

The run-scoped naming contract for the two Playwright suites' raw coverage dumps — consumed by the extension e2e harness and the desktop integration harness alike, so its contract is what those two suite documents state about coverage collection.

Deterministic binaries over the Windows capture layer's pure decisions — native event to action mapping, accessibility-versus-coordinate mode selection, the coordinate helpers with their multi-monitor and DPI math, native element mapping, the platform-agnostic PID base filter, and the scroll accumulator and recording-state transitions. Their contract is the Windows capture doctrine, which states those rules and whose scope-filter row names the PID and Windows-unit binaries as its guards (DCP-5), and the suite orientation whose table lists each binary by name.

The real-input binaries: the integration suite that drives OS input and asserts user actions captured, programmatic effects filtered, the deduplication suppressions, and the OS-chrome and taskbar proxies; and the local-only file-dialog navigation exercise of those same suppressions. Their subject is the core rule separating a user action from an effect and the proxy rules for actions outside the capture layer's view, the Windows specifics beneath them, the retired desktop manual history that names their tests as its replacements, and the suite orientation that lists them.

The capture-layer lifecycle contract binary — idempotent start, no-op stop, the active-state transitions, bounded restart, and the commit flush barrier's sentinel on the action stream — driven entirely through the seam's trait obligations. The capture-seam document states those obligations, the pipeline document owns the barrier and the shutdown doctrine it asserts, and the suite orientation lists it.

The persistence-command binary — the load and save state commands exercised over a redirected application-data directory. The application-shell document owns those commands and their credential-store chokepoint, the persistence document owns the session file they write, and the suite orientation lists it.

The scripted-truth corpus producer for the desktop leg and the desktop conformance-vector fixture: each test drives real OS input through a controlled window and serializes what the capture layer produced. The corpus doctrine owns the session catalogue, the retirement rule, and the vector production; the locator procedure defines the per-strategy element facts the vector fixture emits; and the suite orientation lists it.

The masking and scroll-settling property binaries: a password field's recorded value is always the mask glyph, and a scroll sequence becomes one action only once it settles and clears the displacement floor. Both state cross-platform capture rules — the mask-the-value rule, and the scroll coalescing rule whose row names the scroll binary as a guard (CP-16) — with the Windows specifics beside them, and the suite orientation lists both.

The worker-pool property and truth-lock binary — sequence numbering, shortest-queue dispatch, sticky and drag-pair routing, and the dead-worker drain rescues, alongside end-to-end action truth-locks over the same pipeline. The Windows capture doctrine's ordering row names its flush-barrier tests among that row's existing guards (DCP-2) and the worker-delivery row names its respawn and shutdown drains among that row's (DCP-12), while the drag-classification row's own unit stays intended and names this binary for the right-button path's downstream half alone (DCP-10); the pipeline document owns the delivery model it locks, the retired desktop manual history names it among its replacements, and the suite orientation lists it.

The committed property regression seeds — inputs that once falsified a worker-pool property, replayed on every run. The suite orientation is the one document that names it, stating what the file is and that it stays in the repository.

The extension leg of the scripted-truth corpus: one test per active catalogue session, driving committed input through a fresh persistent context and asserting the comparator's findings against the session's committed baseline. The corpus doctrine owns the sessions, the truth-diff gate, and the produce-stage vector oracle, and its rows name this runner (STC-10, STC-23, STC-24); the end-to-end suite document states the harness contract and the runs that share this tree.

Live conformance-vector production for the corpus run: it snapshots the acted-on frame, marks ground truth by the resolved element's identity, and pairs each mark with the captured action's element facts and locators. The corpus doctrine owns vector production; the locator procedure defines the per-strategy match semantics each snapshot is measured under.

The end-to-end run's configuration — the single worker, the retry budget, the shared teardown, and the trace policy. The end-to-end suite document states that harness contract; the specs the run collects carry their own governing set — declared per spec where its inherited governance reaches past what the extension test area supplies, and that area's own doc set otherwise.

The corpus determinism regime and its vector-producing variant: the fixed viewport, the fixed-port page server, the produce-stage retries around the truth-diff gate, and the flag that turns on vector production with its produced-equals-committed oracle. The corpus doctrine names both configs as the production sites, and the end-to-end suite document states the harness contract they share with the rest of this tree.

The readiness-bound spec: navigation-complete to recorder-ready measured on one machine's clock across the main frame, a srcdoc iframe, and a dynamic subframe, held under half the deliberate-action floor. The extension capture doctrine states that bound and its row names this spec as the guard (ECP-5); the end-to-end suite document lists it and states the harness contract.

Locator emission on live pages: per-strategy match counts and indexes measured over duplicated elements, a duplicated id counted while the derived selector still resolves uniquely, the unique-id fast path, and in-place masking of the value-derived text entry. The locator procedure defines the strategies and the measurement facts it asserts; the end-to-end suite document lists it and states the harness contract.

The registry departure-route spec: the departure routes and the arrival-side lazy reseed pinned through the worker-state introspection handle, with suspension loss simulated and labeled. The extension capture doctrine owns the departure routes and its row names this spec (ECP-3); the extension runtime states the handle's surface, and its persisted-state judgment cites this spec's simulated-loss probes of the rebuildable-state class and the programmatic-tab correlation marker (ERT-1); the extension capture doctrine's exceptions judgment names this spec in its justification (ECP-12); the end-to-end suite document lists it and states the harness contract.

The service-worker end-to-end specs: the message protocol driven from an extension page across the handler surface, and suspension survival — state persisted to extension storage and re-read from it. The extension runtime document owns the dispatcher envelope, the lifecycle and persisted-state model, and the storage write-ownership contract: its persisted-state judgment names the lifecycle spec as the probe of the shipped state's survival (ERT-1), its dispatcher-envelope row names the coverage spec among the interim probes standing in for the unit it still intends (ERT-2), and its write-ownership row names both specs among that row's exercised paths (ERT-3). The end-to-end suite document lists them and states the harness contract.

The storage-pressure spec: a failing write corrupts no stored project, export keeps working, clearing frees space, and the warn-and-pause machine runs through its bands, the user's override, and resume on freed space. The extension capture doctrine states that machine and its row names this spec (ECP-11); the persistence document owns the extension's storage model and its pressure handling; the end-to-end suite document lists it and states the harness contract.

The client-pull guard against a stale bundled seed sample: the real extension pulls a seeded project from a running reference server, reconciles its own platform's sample, and rejects the other platform's as a stamp mismatch. The sync protocol defines the pull, the stamp check, and the skip-and-report handling it asserts; the end-to-end suite document lists it and states the harness contract.

The Chrome adapter's unit suite — settings, sync settings, theme, recording mode, reading guidance, schema loading, the pending-count and action-event subscriptions, and send. The shared-core document owns the platform-adapter seam it implements; the extension runtime document owns the storage write-ownership contract its reads and writes run under, and names this suite among that row's exercised paths (ERT-3); and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The extension background Auto-Sync host: the backstop alarm and data-event triggers wired in the service worker, one shared cycle through the shared store, and the resulting state persisted for the panel to read. The sync protocol owns the trigger set, the backstop interval, and the cycle policy, with a row naming the background host as its interim probe (SP-21); the extension runtime owns the service-worker lifecycle the host runs in; the shared-core document owns the one-implementation seam the cycle goes through; and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The dispatch payload and dispatch-UI suites: the wrapper's fields and their fidelity, the authorization header's presence and omission, endpoint-URL validation, and the panel's send gate — button state, recording selection, the confirmation summary, and the cancel path. The dispatch protocol defines all of it, and its rows name the payload suite as a guard (DI-2, DI-3, DI-4, DI-10); the unit-suite orientation lists them.

Extension capture guards: the per-frame trust predicate deciding whether an appended action may enter a recording, and the static-source guard keeping the background entry module free of dynamic import. The extension capture doctrine states both rules and its rows name both suites (ECP-1, ECP-3); the unit-suite orientation lists them.

The extracted content-script logic: selector derivation, locator measurement over a fake document, element description, and the scroll-capture decision. The cross-platform capture doctrine states the scroll settle-and-floor rule whose row names this suite (CP-16), the extension capture doctrine owns the recorder's own rules, the locator procedure defines the strategies and measurement facts it derives, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The at-rest settings-encryption suite: the envelope shape, the absence of plaintext, the round trip, the path taken once the ephemeral key is gone after a restart, and rejection of tampered ciphertext. The persistence document owns the extension's ephemeral session-storage key and the encrypted settings it protects, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The service-worker handler suite: the panel message protocol over project, recording, and step operations, import and export, the trusted-sender gate on an appended action, redaction of value-derived locator entries, and storage-failure recovery. The extension runtime owns the dispatcher envelope and the handler surface, with a row naming this suite (ERT-2); the extension capture doctrine owns the trust gate and the masking it asserts; the sufficiency-lint document owns the value-derived strategy set the redaction cases read (SL-4); and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The desktop panel's dispatch and sync integration spec: the endpoint gate on the dispatch button, the confirmation surface and its step summary, settings persistence, the sync button, and the re-record and delete flows. The dispatch protocol defines the endpoint rules, the transport seam, and the confirmation surface, with rows naming this spec (DI-10, DI-12, DI-13); the sync protocol defines the cycle the sync button starts; the integration-suite document owns the mocked-backend harness and lists it.

The desktop integration run's configuration — the single worker, the retry budget, headless mode, and the shared teardown that merges the run's coverage. The integration-suite document states that harness contract; the specs the run collects carry their own governing set — declared per spec where its inherited governance reaches past what the desktop test area supplies, and that area's own doc set otherwise.

The Tauri adapter's unit suite — settings, sync settings, theme, recording mode, reading guidance, schema loading, send, the completeness-barrier wrappers around commit and stop, and the redaction pass that leaves locators and provider facts untouched. The application-shell document owns the command surface and the barrier report those wrappers read, the shared-core document owns the platform-adapter seam it implements, the sufficiency-lint document owns the value-derived strategy set the redaction case reads (SL-4), and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The desktop background Auto-Sync host: one shared cycle with the same adapters the manual path uses, the backstop and data-event triggers coalesced through the shared scheduler, triggers dropped while capture is active, and the auth-disable and transient-retry policy. The sync protocol owns the trigger set, the enable rule, and the failure policy, with rows naming the desktop background host (SP-21, SP-23); the shared-core document owns the one-implementation seam the cycle runs through; and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The desktop dispatch service's unit suite — dispatch settings loaded and saved through the backend, the reading guidance carried with a payload, and schema loading. The dispatch protocol defines the endpoint policy and the payload wrapper they serve, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The desktop export suite: a built export validates against the composed platform schema contract and carries every recording, each recording's full step history, and the project metadata. The session-format document defines the export structure and the stamp it carries, the dispatch protocol's wrapper row names this suite for the export contrast it draws (DI-3), and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The desktop persistence module's unit suite — the empty state, serialization and deserialization, and the load and save paths through the backend commands. The persistence document owns the session file and the credential-store split, the application-shell document owns the persistence commands it drives, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The session-state round-trip property: serializing a state and reading it back yields an equivalent state. The persistence document owns the session file whose round trip it pins, and the unit-suite orientation lists it.

The ordered-insertion suite over the desktop adapter: out-of-order events placed by sequence id, immediate delivery with no buffering, completeness, and the internal id stripped before store or export. The Windows capture doctrine states that ordering rule and its row names this suite (DCP-2); the pipeline document owns the delivery model it sits at the end of; and the unit-suite orientation lists it.
